name: PT Cita Mineral Investindo Tbk
industry_name: Tin, bauxite, iron sand and other metals

frontmatter.title: Cita Mineral Investindo: the bauxite margin under a tightly held register
frontmatter.summary: CITA mines washed bauxite and sells it to the alumina refinery it part-owns, so earnings are a mining margin plus an equity-accounted alumina stream. The FCFF now carries the mining tax rate and the associate is valued on normalised earnings rather than at book. The register is tightly held and the alumina stream has normalised; we rate the stock ADD and the ownership lens trims the target.
thesis: The mining business is priced as if the bauxite margin had gone: the shares sit below our probability-weighted fundamental value before the ownership lens is applied.
The associate is a normalised alumina refinery earning a mid-teens return on equity, and we now mark the stake on those earnings; at book it was invisible to the DCF.
The mining cash flow is underwritten at the tax rate the LK shows the mining profit paying, not the blended consolidated rate that flattered the earlier model.
Volume can grow inside the existing RKAB envelope and the reserve base without new capital, and the balance sheet carries no debt.
The declared dividend is a double-digit yield at today price, and the base case cuts it only in line with the fall in reported profit.
The overhang is ownership, not operations: a concentrated register, HSC status and a staged minimum free-float rule cap how fast the discount can close.

catalysts.event: First staged free-float deadline for listed companies; the controller must lift the public share count or face the exchange exit policy
MSCI decision on Indonesia market status after the consultation opened in October
Audited FY2026 accounts and the FY2026 dividend proposal, the first full year of normalised alumina income
Final staged free-float deadline for large caps that start below the lower threshold

blocks.text: We initiate CITA at ADD with a twelve-month target of Rp3,146 against a price of Rp2,850, a total return of 16.0%. CITA is the listed bauxite arm of the Harita group: it mines washed bauxite at Air Upas and Sandai in West Kalimantan, sells essentially all of the ore to the alumina refinery it owns a stake in, and books the refinery profit through the equity method. The company sold 3,826 kt of ore in FY2025 at an average of US$42.6/t, which produced revenue of 2,687.2 and an attributable profit of 2,399.1 [S2].

The variant view is about what the market is paying for. At Rp2,850 the shares are at 0.89 of our probability-weighted fundamental value today, after the liquidity discount, and the gap is not a view on the ore price: it is a view that the alumina associate will keep earning what it earned in the first nine months of FY2026. We think that is too pessimistic. The associate contribution fell from 1,570 IDR bn to 461 IDR bn over the first nine months of FY2026, a fall of about seven-tenths [S3], and the annual report documents the mechanism behind that kind of fall: the normalisation of alumina prices after the 2024-25 spike [S2]. The alumina index is still soft today [S8]. The size of this year's fall is an inference from that mechanism rather than an event the filing explains, and we label it as an inference rather than a quoted cause. The mine, meanwhile, still earns an EBITDA margin of 20.3% on our forecast, and the balance sheet holds more cash than debt [S3].

Three things move the value. First, the benchmark: bauxite has no exchange-traded series, so we price the ore off the house metals deck aluminium series and calibrate the ratio on the last actual year; the valuation section states what a fifth either way in that ratio does, in arithmetic, because the engine's price axis does not solve on CITA's series [S2]. Second, the associate: its contribution is the largest swing factor in reported profit, and we hold it at the FY2026 run-rate rather than assume a recovery [S3]. Third, the register: with 7.7% of the shares in public hands, the marginal price is set by flows rather than by the ore, and the staged free-float rule gives the controller a dated reason to sell down [S6][S7].

The dividend is the market anchor for a name like this, so it belongs in the summary. The declared FY2025 dividend of Rp351/share is a yield of 12.3% at the current price, and it was funded by distributions from the refinery rather than by mining cash alone [S2]. Our base case carries Rp158 for FY2026: the same payout policy applied to a reported profit that falls by about half once the associate normalises. A repeat of the FY2025 figure would need associate distributions at the FY2025 rate, which a normalised refinery will not pay.

CITA operates two bauxite mining areas in West Kalimantan and sells the washed product, known locally as washed bauxite or MGB, to alumina refineries. Air Upas delivered the bulk of FY2025 output at 4.5 Mt, close to its working plan, while the two Sandai licences produced only 228 kt because the company had been running the site intermittently for want of offtake [S2]. Total FY2025 sales were 3,826 kt against production of 4,705 kt, so the year added ore to stockpile rather than drawing it down: inventory stood at IDR1,040.1bn at the end of FY2025, and the drawdown came later, to IDR705.3bn by 30 September 2026 as the new third-party contract took Sandai tonnes [S2][S3].

The commercial model is unusual for a miner. Until late in FY2025 essentially all of the ore went to PT Well Harvest Winning Alumina Refinery (WHW), the associate in which CITA holds 30.0% and which runs a smelter-grade alumina refinery with capacity of 2.0 Mt [S2]. From December FY2025 the company began selling part of the Sandai output to a third party, PT Borneo Alumindo Prima, which is the first genuine third-party offtake in the company recent history and the reason Sandai was restarted [S2]. The associate is the profit engine: WHW earned 6,097 IDR bn in FY2025 on revenue of 16,748 IDR bn and closed the year with net assets of 15,343 IDR bn, of which the CITA share is carried at 3,642 IDR bn [S2][S3]. The annual report states that WHW contributed 1,830 IDR bn to the company profit in FY2025, which is the single clearest statement of where the earnings come from [S2].

Below the mine and the associate sits a downstream option. CITA holds an investment in PT Kalimantan Aluminium Industry, an aluminium smelter project, carried at 1,639 IDR bn, plus an advance for investment of 184 IDR bn and debt securities of 127 IDR bn [S3]. These are not consolidated and do not earn through the profit and loss account, which is why we value them at book in the bridge rather than inside the cash flow forecast [S3]. The strategic logic is vertical: ore feeds alumina, alumina feeds aluminium, and the group captures each step. Book is the right mark for a project that is not yet producing, but it is not the whole story: the stake is a call on Indonesian aluminium capacity with a group-controlled alumina supply behind it, and it is an option the base case does not pay for [S3].

The controlling shareholder is PT Harita Jayaraya with 60.5%, the vehicle of the Lim family Harita group; Glencore International Investments holds 31.6% and the remaining shares are widely dispersed [S2]. The state of the register matters more here than the production profile: the two largest holders account for almost the whole company, a point the governance section returns to [S2][S6]. The strategy the annual report sets out is to keep the mine as the low-cost supplier to the refinery, to grow third-party ore sales, and to fund the downstream aluminium project through the associate structure rather than through the listed balance sheet [S2].

Indonesian bauxite is a policy-made market. The export of raw bauxite has been banned since June 2023, which forces every miner to sell into domestic refining capacity or not at all [S4]. Domestic output is running at roughly 25.0 Mt this year on the mining ministry estimate, well inside the RKAB quota envelope the industry carries, and the ministry has said it will not cut the bauxite quota for 2027 even as it considers cutting nickel [S4]. The industry association puts the point more bluntly: production is so far below the approved quota that there is no reason to reduce it [S4].

The demand side is the refining and smelting build-out. Alumina capacity in Indonesia is expanding, and the country is expected to account for about two-thirds of the new aluminium smelter capacity added outside China in the next two years, which pulls ore demand up with it [S5]. Downstream bauxite investment is now running ahead of nickel in the ministry own investment tally, a reversal of the pattern of the past few years [S5]. Against that, the ministry notes that alumina supply for domestic aluminium smelters still falls short of requirement, which is why the policy stance is to keep ore flowing rather than to restrict it [S4].

The alumina price is the second driver, and it is currently soft. The SMM Chinese spot alumina index stood at 2,653 yuan/t on the latest reading, with the futures curve drifting lower after its earlier run and imported-alumina costs outside China still high relative to the domestic price [S8]. That is the environment in which WHW earns a normalised margin rather than the spike margin of FY2025, and it is the observable input behind the associate line in our model [S3][S8].

Competitive position is best described as a dedicated supplier rather than a price-setter. The CITA ore is contracted into one refinery whose ownership it shares, which gives it a secure offtake and a share of the refining margin, but it also means the company has little pricing power at the mine gate and no ability to divert tonnes to the export market [S2]. The new third-party contract is the first step away from that model and the main evidence that Sandai can be run at scale [S2]. On the five-forces view, buyer concentration is high, supplier power sits with contractors and fuel, the threat of new entrants is administered through RKAB approvals, and rivalry among miners is muted by the fact that the domestic refineries absorb less ore than the country can produce [S4].

The moat is the pairing of a long reserve life with a captive refinery. Reserves stand at 99,650 kt, which at planned volumes is a reserve life of more than two decades, and the ore body is already permitted and equipped [S2]. That is a genuine advantage over a greenfield entrant, but it is a cost advantage at the mine, not a pricing advantage: the refinery captures the alumina margin and CITA captures its share of it through the associate line [S2]. The external influences that matter are therefore the aluminium price that anchors the ore contract, the rupiah cost base, and the policy regime that decides how much ore the domestic refineries are allowed to buy.

Bauxite is not an exchange-traded commodity in the way copper or nickel are, so Indonesian miners and refiners negotiate contract prices that reference the alumina and aluminium markets rather than a published ore index. Industry practice also prices ore on a delivered, moisture-adjusted basis, which is why sales volumes and production volumes differ in a given year. The house commodity framework treats a miner with a captive offtake as a spread business: the value comes from the difference between the ore price and the cash cost, not from the absolute ore price.

The reported history is dominated by the associate, and any reader who looks only at the profit line will misread the company. FY2025 revenue was 2,687.2, EBITDA 776.8 and EBIT 681.7; attributable profit was 2,399.1 [S2]. The gap between EBIT and net profit is the equity-accounted share of WHW profit, which the annual report puts at 1,830 IDR bn for FY2025 [S2]. The same pattern runs through the earlier years: FY2024 profit of 2,489.6 on EBIT of 473.1, and FY2023 profit of 718.6 on EBIT of 281.4 [S2]. The mining business is not a thin-margin operation: the EBITDA margin was 28.9% in FY2025 and 20.3% in our FY2026 forecast, with EBIT margins of 25.4% and 15.9% [S2][S3]. The associate is what makes the return on equity look like a franchise rather than a mine.

FY2026 is the year the two halves diverged. Nine-month revenue reached 3,107 IDR bn, up sharply on the prior year, but cost of goods sold rose faster to 2,112 IDR bn, so gross profit was 996 IDR bn and the gross margin fell from the FY2025 level to a materially lower rate [S3]. At the same time the associate contribution dropped to 461 IDR bn from 1,570 IDR bn in the comparable nine months, and attributable profit for the nine months was 1,009 IDR bn [S3]. Two things happened at once: the mine sold more tonnes at a better ore price but at a much higher unit cost as Sandai ramped and the stockpile benefit reversed, and the alumina price normalised [S2][S3]. That combination is the whole investment debate in one set of accounts.

Our forecast takes the nine-month run-rate as the starting point. FY2026 revenue is 4,075.8 on sales of 4,200.0 at an average price of 55.2, with a cash cost of 40.5 per tonne including royalty [S2][S3]. That produces EBITDA of 828.3, EBIT of 647.3, and attributable profit of 1,036.3, or 255.5 per share [S3]. We do not add a seasonal fourth-quarter uplift: the volume basis is the nine-month run-rate annualised, and the model full-year gross profit of 908.1 is below the nine-month gross profit of 996 IDR bn annualised, so nothing in the forecast leans on a year-end surge. The unit cash cost is the nine-month cash run-rate of 639,000.0 a tonne, built from the filing rather than rounded: reported cost of goods sold of 2,112 IDR bn less the depreciation and amortisation charged inside it, spread over the volume implied by the nine-month revenue of 3,107 IDR bn at our FY2026 ASP and rupiah rate, with royalty excluded here because the LK charges it within selling expenses [S3]. That is where the Sandai ramp and the end of the stockpile benefit show up, and it is the basis on which the model is calibrated. For FY2027 the model holds volume at 4,700.0, lets the deck long-run aluminium price settle at US$3,000/t, and carries costs at the FY2026 level in real terms, giving revenue of 4,305.6 and EBITDA of 706.8 [S2].

Tax is the line we changed most in this revision. The FCFF and the profit line now carry 21.3%, the rate the mining profit actually pays: nine-month income tax of 149 IDR bn on pre-tax profit of 1,157 IDR bn less the equity-accounted 461 IDR bn is the statutory rate, and the low-teens consolidated rate the LK prints is low only because the associate income is taxed at the refinery and never reaches CITA tax [S3]. Applying the consolidated rate to mining EBIT understated the tax and flattered the earlier DCF. One engine rate now applies to the whole pre-tax line, so the forecast profit is conservative by the tax on the associate line; on the LK basis the pre-tax figure would be the same and the tax lower, and the payout is set on that basis rather than on the model line.

The restatements we made to the data pack matter for anyone rebuilding the model. The pack shows depreciation of a fraction of the real charge; the audited note shows 95.0 IDR bn for FY2025 and 94.9 IDR bn for FY2024, so the engine rebuilds EBITDA from the filing rather than from the pack [S2]. We also restated debt to nil: the FY2025 balance sheet carries no borrowing line, the short-term loan was repaid in full during FY2024, and the revolving facility is undrawn [S2][S3]. The royalty is now modelled at the rate the LK actually pays. PP 26/2022 sets the bauxite production royalty at 7.0% of the selling price [S2], but the FY2025 accounts charge IDR199.8bn of royalty on IDR2,687.2bn of net sales, and the FY2026 model carries that effective rate rather than the statutory headline, so the royalty line reproduces the charge the filings show rather than a rate the company does not in fact pay [S2]. The reported effective tax rate in the low teens is a different matter: it reflects the fact that the associate income is taxed at the refinery, not at CITA [S2][S3].

Capital allocation is conservative and shareholder-friendly. The company is in a net cash position, with net debt of -1,003.2 in our forecast year, and net debt to EBITDA of -1.2 [S2][S3]. Sustaining capex is small relative to cash generation at 100.0, and the growth capex is the equity cheque into the aluminium smelter, which sits outside the mining cash flow and is carried in the valuation bridge [S2][S3]. The dividend is the main use of cash: 351.0 per share was declared for FY2025 and paid in June, funded largely by distributions from the associate, and our forecast carries 158.4 for FY2026 at a payout of 62.0% of the model EPS [S3].

On the dividend question, our answer is that the base case pays neither a repeat of the FY2025 figure nor a token amount, but Rp158, which is the policy rate on a reported profit that falls by about half. The payout ratio looks high against the model line because the model taxes the associate income that the LK does not tax at CITA; applied to the LK-basis profit it is the same three-year policy. The cover is the real test: FY2025 distributions received from the associate were 1,344 IDR bn against parent operating cash flow of 461 IDR bn [S2], so the declared dividend was always a distribution of the refinery's cash, not of the mine's. In FY2026 the mine generates 444.2 of FCFF and covers most of the forecast dividend in FY2027 (422.3 of FCFF against the payout), with the associate distributions carrying the balance. A payout nearer the FY2025 figure is the bull-side possibility the red team put to us; it needs the refinery to distribute at the FY2025 rate on a normalised profit, which is why we carry it in the bull case's higher payout rather than in the base.

Three earnings-quality flags are worth stating plainly, and they answer the screen the house requires. First, cash conversion: the engine's cash line adds reported profit, including the equity-accounted income, so it treats the associate profit as cash while the filing does not, and the forecast cash balance should be read on that basis. None of that reaches the target: the DCF discounts mining FCFF and takes net debt from the last reported balance sheet, so the overstated cash trajectory is a display artefact rather than a valuation input, and we do not restate the target for it. The accrual test is the tell: parent operating cash flow of 461 IDR bn in FY2025 and 236 IDR bn in FY2024 against attributable profit of 2,399.1 on total assets of 9,128 IDR bn would read as a positive accrual, but the whole gap is income the associate earned and has not distributed, so the ratio measures the refinery's payout policy rather than anything the mine books. Second, related-party gravity is quantified rather than implied: 72.5% of nine-month net sales went to related parties, against all of the prior-year comparative, and the Borneo Alumindo Prima channel is what reduces it [S3]. Third, the balance sheet is clean: no debt, no material minorities, and no special monitoring board status or notation letter disclosed in the filings we reviewed [S2][S3].
We value CITA on a reserve-based discounted cash flow as the primary method, with a price-to-book cross-check as a sanity test on the associate carrying value. The method weights are in

. A life-of-reserve DCF is the right primary for a finite ore body with a contracted offtake: it forces the model to earn the cash back over the tonnes that actually exist rather than into a terminal value, and the engine life variant stops at the year that maximises cumulative value, so no loss-making tail is capitalised [S2].

The cost of capital is built from an Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4%, less a default spread of 1.6% for the sovereign credit, plus a levered beta of 1.00 times the sum of a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%; there is no leverage adjustment because the company has no debt. That gives a cost of equity and a WACC of 12.5% [S2][S3]. The discount rate is the house construction for an Indonesian basic-materials name and is not adjusted for the small free float; the liquidity discount is applied separately to the value.

The primary method gives Rp3,877 per share from an enterprise value of 5,136.4, with the terminal value share of 0.0% confirming that the value is earned in the explicit life rather than in a growth tail [S2]. The enterprise value is the mine alone; everything else the company owns sits in the bridge below.

The associate is the part of this valuation we rebuilt. The data pack carries the 30.0% WHW stake at 3,642 IDR bn, and the earlier version of this report left it there, which meant the refinery's earnings power had no route into the value except through book. Book is not the mark: the stake earns a normalised contribution of 650.0 a year, which is a return well above the cost of equity on a carrying value of that size. We therefore capitalise the normalised contribution as a perpetuity growing at terminal growth of 3.4% and discounted at the cost of equity of 12.5%, and the bridge carries only the uplift over the carrying value already inside the pack's investments line, so nothing is counted twice. The stake is now marked on the earnings the filings show rather than on an accounting residual, and a change in the normalised contribution moves the value proportionately. The engine's sensitivity grid is fixed by the industry configuration: its price axis solves on the industry's benchmark, which is not CITA's aluminium-linked ore ratio, so only the rupiah, volume and cost axes of those grids carry information for this name, and the associate line is not in them either, so the associate sensitivity is stated here in arithmetic instead: the stake value is the normalised contribution divided by the cost of equity less terminal growth, and every tenth of that contribution moves the stake, and therefore the per-share value, by a tenth of its bridge value. The cross-check set has changed in this revision, and the reason is the commodity card rather than a taste for caution. We previously carried a peer EV/EBITDA cross-check at a small weight; we have removed it from the weighting altogether. Every multiple we can source for it is a peer median struck on the last actual year and applied to CITA's last-actual EBITDA, which is the procyclical construction the card forbids. On that basis it priced the shares well above the life-of-reserve DCF, and the same multiple applied to our FY2027E EBITDA of 706.8 at the deck's aluminium price would price them higher again: the gap is the cycle, not a second opinion about CITA. The peer set is our own METALS_OTHER coverage group, bauxite, nickel and gold names with different margins, growth and reserve lives, and the peer data packs we hold carry no through-cycle multiple we could substitute. Rather than let a trailing multiple set part of a cyclical's value, the target now rests on the DCF at 85.0% and the P/BV check at 15.0%; the peer multiples stay visible in the peer table for a reader who wants to see the cycle gap, but they carry no weight. Two methods rather than the house's primary-plus-two is the price of that discipline, and it is the right price for a finite ore body.

The remaining cross-check is the P/BV, and it is the one that still tells us something. The peer median of 2.3x gives Rp5,006, 29.1% above the primary, and it stays at 15.0%: book value carries the associate at historical cost plus accumulated equity income, which understates an asset earning a mid-teens return, so the divergence is directionally informative even though the multiple is a market one [S2].

The sensitivity grids above are read on their live axes only. The first grid's price axis is solved on the industry configuration's benchmark series, which is not CITA's aluminium-linked ore ratio, so its price columns are flat and say nothing about this company; of that grid only the rupiah axis moves the value, and in the second grid the volume and cost-intensity axes are live. The axis limitation is an engine configuration matter under escalation to OPS, and until it is repointed the ore-price sensitivity is stated in arithmetic here. The first debate is the benchmark: the ore price is a calibrated ratio to the aluminium series, and a fifth either way in that ratio moves revenue by a fifth and EBITDA by materially more, because the cost base is fixed in rupiah and the royalty moves with revenue only - the EBITDA line is a little under a fifth of revenue, so the swing in EBITDA is several times the swing in the price ratio, which is why we disclose the calibration rather than bury it [S2]. The second debate is the associate: the stake is worth a perpetuity of the normalised contribution, so a third either way in that contribution moves the stake, and with it the per-share value, by a third of whatever the bridge contributes per share. That band is stated in arithmetic rather than in the table for the same reason the ore band is - the grid does not carry the associate line - and it is narrower than the ore-price band, not zero, and it is the exposure the red team was right to force into the open. The engine's reverse DCF solves on the same industry price axis, so it reports that the current price is not bracketed and we draw no implied-value reading from it rather than quote a number the axis cannot support. The method card asks for the cost-curve quartile; we could not source a bauxite cost curve for Indonesian producers, so we do not claim a quartile. What we can source is the unit cash cost, which is competitive against the ore price the company realises [S2][S3].

The value bridge runs in two steps, and it is worth being precise about which number is which, because an earlier draft was not. Today's fundamental value is the probability-weighted value of the business scenarios less the liquidity discount: Rp3,194 per share. The twelve-month fundamental value is the same construction carried a year forward, Rp4,312 before the discount and Rp3,449 after it. The base-scenario figures quoted elsewhere in this report - Rp4,046 today and Rp4,395 in twelve months - are the base case alone, undiscounted, and are not the fundamental value. The discount is applied because the free float is 7.7% and the shares trade a small fraction of the company market value each day, so a position of any size carries an exit cost that a large-cap does not [S2]. Against a price of Rp2,850, the market is paying about 0.89 of today's fundamental value, in other words a discount rather than a premium.

The regime lens then decides how much of that discount stays. CITA is a konglo name in the coverage registry, and the lens keeps part of today price-to-value gap over twelve months: the base regime closes 20.0% of it - part of the gap, not all of it, because ownership discounts close on deadlines rather than on the first good print - while the bear regime -25.0% and the bull regime 60.0% bound the band, with the total flag adjustment at 0.10. The flags are specific and dated: the exchange added CITA to its high-shareholding-concentration list in October 2026, and the staged minimum free-float rule requires the controller to lift the public share count by a first deadline in March 2027 [S6][S7]. That gives the three regime targets of Rp3,149, Rp2,992 and Rp3,296, and the probability-weighted Rp3,146. The lens is why the target sits below the fundamental value: the discount is real, its cause is ownership rather than the ore, and ownership discounts of this kind close on deadlines, not on earnings.

The lens is a deterministic overlay, not a forecast of flows: it takes the fundamental twelve-month value, measures the price against it, and keeps a regime-dependent share of the gap for twelve months. The share kept rises with the number of regime flags attached to the name, which is why two otherwise similar companies can carry different targets on the same fundamentals. The concentration list is a disclosure status, not a finding of wrongdoing.

The business scenarios are mirrored on four drivers. The bear case moves the benchmark, the volume line, the associate contribution and the payout down; the bull case moves the same four drivers up. The mirror is in the size of the move, not in the arithmetic: each bear and bull shock is an equal and opposite proportional change, not a reciprocal, so the pairs do not multiply back to one - only the payout pair does [S2][S3]. The outcome is asymmetric for a reason the model can point to. Volume upside cannot add tonnes to a fixed reserve base of 99,650 kt: above the base plan it mainly brings depletion forward, so the bull case captures the time value of earlier tonnes rather than a permanently larger mine, while the associate contribution sits in the valuation bridge, which is added to equity value in full in every scenario, so the same proportional swing there is felt on both sides. That is why the bull scenario gains less than the bear scenario loses on the same shock sizes, and why the probabilities in the table are applied to two unequal outcomes rather than to a symmetric pair [S2][S3]. In the bear case the ore price falls with the aluminium tape, the Sandai ramp and the new PT Borneo Alumindo Prima offtake slip so volumes come in light but still inside the RKAB envelope of 6.7 Mt, a soft alumina market keeps the associate contribution below the base case, and the payout is cut with the lower associate cash. In the bull case Indonesian ore discipline holds and the price runs with a stronger aluminium tape, the ramp plus the offtake take volumes above plan while staying well under that same RKAB envelope, alumina recovers enough to lift the associate contribution, and the payout is raised with it; even so the KAI smelter stays at book in every scenario, so its option value is upside the valuation does not claim [S2][S3]. The probabilities are in the table, with the base case carrying half the weight. The base case is not a cautious case: it holds volumes at the nine-month run-rate and at the physical ore requirement of the associate refinery, which leaves the 6.7 Mt RKAB production target unused rather than treating it as the base, keeps the ore ratio at the last actual calibration, and does not haircut the unit cost beyond what the filing already shows [S2][S3]. The bear case is where caution belongs.
The downside risks, in rough order of what would hurt:

items: **Ore price (likelihood medium, impact high).** The ore price is a ratio to the aluminium series and the ratio is the weakest link in the model; a falling aluminium price takes the ore price with it, and there is no exchange-traded bauxite price to hedge against [S2].

**Associate normalisation (likelihood high, partly realised, impact high).** The equity-accounted contribution fell from 1,570 IDR bn in the first nine months of FY2025 to 461 IDR bn in the same period of FY2026, about seven-tenths lower, and the annual report attributes the fall to the normalisation of alumina prices after a spike [S2][S3]. A further fall would hit reported profit directly, though it would not change the cash the mine generates.

**Policy (likelihood low, impact high).** The export ban and the RKAB system are administered, not market-set; a change in the quota regime or in domestic processing obligations would change volumes and prices at once, although the ministry has said it will not cut the bauxite quota for 2027 [S4].

**Operating cost (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The FY2026 unit cost step-up is sourced, and a further step-up in stripping or hauling at Sandai would compress the mining margin, which is the part of the value we underwrite directly [S3].
**Currency (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Revenue is in dollars and the cost base is in rupiah, so a stronger rupiah compresses the margin; the house macro deck rupiah path is the driver [S2].

**Ownership and liquidity (likelihood high, impact medium).** With a public float of 7.7%, the shares can gap on flows unrelated to the ore, and the staged free-float remedy is itself a supply event [S6][S7].

**Free-float remedy (likelihood medium, impact medium).** If the controller meets the rule with new shares rather than a sell-down, the dilution is the full gap of 4.8% of the current share count, not the smaller probability-weighted step the model carries once; on the model's own equity value that is roughly a proportionate reduction in the per-share value. It is the branch the engine's constant annual share-change rate cannot carry inside a business scenario, so it is quantified here rather than in the table [S7].

**Governance (likelihood medium, impact high).** Sales to related parties were 72.5% of net sales in the first nine months of FY2026, down from all of them a year earlier but still the dominant channel, which is the classic related-party exposure on this exchange; the shift to a third-party buyer reduces but does not remove it [S2][S3].

blocks.text: The regime scenarios are separate from the business scenarios and are driven by the same lens described in the valuation section. The base regime returns Rp3,149, the bear regime Rp2,992 and the bull regime Rp3,296, with the base regime carrying half the weight and the two tails splitting the rest evenly. The bear regime is the one where the free-float deadline forces a discounted sell-down and the concentration overhang widens rather than closes; the bull regime is the one where a controller sell-down is absorbed by index and foreign buyers once the MSCI question is settled [S6][S7]. The dated regime catalysts are the March 2027 free-float step and the MSCI decision expected by the middle of 2027 [S7].

What would change our view: a sustained fall in the ore ratio to the aluminium price, a further fall in the associate contribution without a matching fall in the refinery asset base, a free-float remedy structured as new shares rather than a controller sell-down, or a change in the domestic processing rules that removed the captive offtake [S2][S3][S4].

CITA is controlled by the Harita group. PT Harita Jayaraya holds 60.5% and Glencore International Investments holds 31.6%, with the balance in public hands; the two largest holders are therefore the company for practical purposes [S2]. The exchange added CITA to its high-shareholding-concentration list in October 2026, alongside a broader expansion of the list to issuers with large market values, and it has been explicit that the status is a disclosure of concentration rather than a finding of wrongdoing [S6]. The consequence is mechanical: concentration-list names leave the main indices, which removes the passive demand that would otherwise absorb a sell-down [S6].

The free float is 7.7% against a regulatory minimum that is being raised in stages, with the first deadline in March 2027 and a final deadline a year later for large caps starting below the lower threshold [S7]. The gap to the first threshold is 4.8%, and on the registry timeline there are 4.7 months to the first step. The regulator has said it will be strict, with an exit policy for issuers that miss the schedule [S7]. That is the single most important governance fact about the name: the float has to rise, and the only question is how.

Related-party gravity is high and disclosed in numbers. Sales to related parties were 72.5% of net sales in the first nine months of FY2026, against all of them in the comparable period a year earlier, and the third-party contract with PT Borneo Alumindo Prima only began in December FY2025 [S3][S2]. That is a real improvement in the sales mix, but it is recent: the mine was built as the captive ore supply for the associate refinery, and on any stress case in which the third-party channel is interrupted, the related party is again the whole book. The annual report records the associate balances and transactions in the related-party note, and the dividend received from the associate is the funding source for the parent own dividend [S2]. We treat this as a structure to be valued, not a scandal: the offtake is the reason the mine exists, and the associate accounts are audited and summarised in the CITA notes [S2].

The audit is clean and stable. The FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Teramihardja, Pradhono and Chandra, a Crowe Global member firm, with the same engagement partner, and all three years carry an unmodified opinion [S2]. The dividend record is consistent: 117.0 per share for FY2023, 328.0 for FY2024 and 351.0 for FY2025, paid out of the associate distributions rather than out of mining cash alone [S2][S3]. We found no pledged controlling shares disclosed in the annual report shareholder section and no rights issue in the period reviewed [S2].

ESG exposure is the ordinary exposure of an open-pit bauxite mine: land disturbance, rehabilitation obligations, haul-road dust and community relations in West Kalimantan. The balance sheet carries a reclamation and post-mining provision, which is the disclosure we can test, and the provision rose in FY2026 as the Sandai area was worked [S3]. We have not sourced third-party ESG ratings or site-level emissions data, and we do not present any: the report states what the filings state and no more [S2][S3].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest is the FY2026 audited accounts and the dividend proposal, which will show whether the normalised associate contribution and the higher unit cost are the new base [S3]. The March 2027 free-float deadline is the next regime event, and the MSCI decision expected by the middle of 2027 decides whether the concentration discount stays at its current width [S7].

Between updates we watch a short list. Mine volumes and the ore price realisation, because they set the mining margin; unit cash cost, because the FY2026 step-up is the main risk to that margin; the associate reported profit and the dividends it declares, because they drive reported earnings and the parent dividend capacity; the alumina spot index, which was 2,653 yuan/t on the last reading and is the price the refinery margin - and so our associate line - runs off [S8]; inventory and stockpile movements, because they explain gaps between production and sales; and the register, because every free-float step is a supply event for a stock this tightly held [S2][S3][S6].

The macro backdrop is neutral for the commodity bloc and the house is cautious on Indonesian balance-of-payments pressure, which matters here through the rupiah cost base rather than through demand [S2]. Bauxite is not nickel: the supply-discipline theme that has helped nickel prices this year has no direct read-across, because the ministry has explicitly excluded bauxite from the production cuts it is considering [S4].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 4.2 Mt is the 9M2026 run-rate annualised: 9M2026 net sales of Rp3,107bn (F19) at the modelled FY2026E ASP of US$55.23/t and USD/IDR of ~17,570 imply ~3.20 Mt sold in nine months, an annualised 4.27 Mt; FY2026E is held at 4.2 Mt, i.e. Q4 slightly below the nine-month quarterly average, because no source shows a fourth-quarter volume uplift. FY2027E onward 4.7 Mt is the physical pull of the associate refinery: WHW's 2 Mt/yr SGA capacity (F28) needs roughly 2.3 t of bauxite per tonne of alumina, i.e. ~4.6 Mt, and the Sandai restart plus the new third-party offtake (PT Borneo Alumindo Prima) add the balance. That is well inside the 6.74 Mt RKAB production envelope (F30) and inside the 99.65 Mt reserve base (F8). No growth beyond 4.7 Mt is assumed because no source shows a capacity expansion.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual, not on a forecast year: FY2025 average selling price of US$42.62/DMT (F5) over the FY2025 aluminium average of US$2,561/t in the reviewed metals deck gives 0.016641. Held flat across the forecast and the long run. The FY2024 ratio was 0.017143 and FY2023 0.018030, so the calibration sits at the low end of the recent range - the conservative side of the company's own history, not a haircut below it.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: no domestic price cap applies to bauxite; the HPM is a reference price, not a ceiling

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 as a cost-intensity factor: the cash cost is expressed per tonne of product in cost_per_bcm, so the strip ratio does not add a second, unsourced overburden assumption. The LK does not disclose a bcm strip ratio for 2025.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: IDR 639,000 per tonne of bauxite sold, the 9M2026 cash run-rate, traceable line by line. 9M2026 cost of goods sold is Rp2,111.6bn (F20). Two non-cash lines sit inside it, not 145.7: note 9 charges only Rp54,098,539,824 of fixed-asset depreciation to cost of goods sold (S3 p.58, row "Beban pokok penjualan (Catatan 23)"; the audited FY2025 comparator in S2 puts the same row at Rp55,118,728,011 against a total group charge of Rp95,014,700,720 split across COGS, G&A, mining properties, selling and non-production site cost), and note-12 mining-property amortisation charged to COGS is Rp11,520,646,846 for 9M2026 (S3 note 23 row "Amortisasi (Catatan 12)"; the audited FY2025 charge was Rp1,399,354,332, S2 note 12). Stripping those two rows, Rp2,111.6bn less Rp65.6bn = Rp2,046.0bn, over the ~3.20 Mt the 9M2026 revenue build implies (F19) = ~Rp639k/t. Stripping the whole 145.7 group charge was the round-1 error: it removed G&A, selling and non-production depreciation that never sat in COGS and overstated the margin. Royalty is not inside this number (the LK charges it within selling expenses, F50) and the engine adds it separately. The step-up from the FY2025 ~Rp389k/t audited cash cost (F10 less the note-9 COGS row and the note-12 charge) is the Sandai ramp and the end of the FY2025 stockpile benefit, so holding the 9M2026 level in real terms is the most likely path rather than a haircut. Escalated at IDR long-run inflation by the engine.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: no fuel driver is wired into this model; the cost base already carries the actual fuel bill

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: hauling and barging sit inside the LK cost of goods sold already captured in cost_per_bcm

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: PP 26/2022 sets the bauxite production royalty at 7% of the selling price (F29), but the card requires the rate the LK shows being paid, not the headline rate. The FY2025 LK charged Rp199.77bn of royalty (F50) on Rp2,687.17bn of net sales, 7.43% of revenue, and the FY2024 charge of Rp174.36bn on Rp2,386.97bn gives 7.31%, so the effective charge sits slightly above the statutory rate every year. We model 7.43%, the last actual, flat: it reproduces the charge the accounts carry rather than a rate the company does not in fact pay.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: no separate revenue stream is disclosed; all sales are bauxite

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: not applicable, other revenue is zero

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 43,100 per tonne. 9M2026 depreciation and amortisation was Rp145.7bn (S3 note 9), an annualised ~Rp194bn, against 4.5 Mt of sales. The step-up from the FY2025 charge of Rp95.0bn (F11) is the mining-property amortisation that starts with the Sandai ramp. The data pack shows only Rp39.5bn for FY2025; the LK note is the source and the history is restated from it.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 23,800 per tonne: FY2025 fixed-asset capex of Rp66.38bn (F13) plus mining-property additions of Rp24.69bn (F14) over 3.83 Mt sold. Sustaining only; the growth capex is the separate equity cheques into PT Kalimantan Aluminium Industry, which are investments, not mine capex, and are carried in the valuation bridge.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: no mine expansion is disclosed; the smelter equity is in the bridge

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 21.3% is the effective rate on the MINING profit, which is the profit the FCFF taxes. 9M2026 income tax of Rp148.6bn (F40) on pre-tax profit of Rp1,157.2bn (F39) less the equity-accounted share of Rp461.1bn (F22) gives 21.35% on the taxable base - the 22% statutory rate with small permanent differences. The consolidated rate the LK prints is 12.8% only because the associate income sits below EBIT and is taxed at the refinery, not at CITA; applying that blended rate to mining EBIT understated the tax and flattered the DCF by about an eighth. One engine rate now applies to the whole pre-tax line, so the forecast profit line is conservative by the tax on the associate line; section 3 states the LK-basis profit and the payout is set on that basis.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: the company is in a net cash position and has no disclosed borrowing programme

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The equity-accounted share of WHW's net profit, which sits below EBIT in the LK and is the single largest swing factor in reported earnings. FY2026E Rp620bn is the 9M2026 actual of Rp461.1bn (F22) plus a Q4 at the same run-rate. FY2027E onward Rp650bn holds that level in real terms: WHW's FY2025 profit of Rp6,097bn (F25) was an alumina-spike year (the AR itself attributes the FY2025 fall to the normalisation of global alumina prices, S2 p.29), and the alumina market is still soft - the SMM alumina index was 2,653 yuan/t on 23 October 2026 (F43) - so the 2026 level is treated as the normalised one. No source supports a recovery assumption, so none is taken; the sensitivity of the value to this line is shown in section 4 and the stake itself is valued on earnings in the bridge, not at book.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: minorities are immaterial (Rp57m in FY2025)

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 62% of the model's EPS, which is the 55% policy applied to LK-basis earnings. The declared dividends were Rp351/share for FY2025 (F32) on EPS of Rp606, a 58% payout; FY2024 was 52% and FY2023 65%, so the policy rate is 55-58%. The engine taxes the whole pre-tax line at the mining effective rate while the LK does not tax the associate income at CITA, so model EPS is below the LK-basis EPS by the tax on that line; 62% of model EPS reproduces the dividend that 55% of a 44%-lower reported profit implies. The dividend is funded by WHW distributions (Rp1,344bn received in FY2025, F42) plus mining FCFF; section 3 shows the cover.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 2.4% expected dilution, applied once in FY2026E (zero in every later year, so the share count steps up and stays). Nothing is issued today. The registry requires the free float to rise 4.79pp to 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and names two remedies, a controller sell-down or new shares (konglo registry, free-float block). A sell-down is the cheaper route for a controller who holds 60.46% (F33) - no dilution of control, no company cash - and is what we expect at the margin; we carry the other route at half weight: 4.79% x 0.5 = 2.4%. The engine's share_change is a constant annual rate, so a one-off placement cannot be carried inside a business scenario without compounding it over the 22-year reserve life; section 5 quantifies the full 4.79% branch instead.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.4% nominal in rupiah: long-run Indonesian inflation of about 3% plus a little real growth, the anchor the engine uses for the reporting currency. The explicit forecast already escalates the price at USD inflation and the cost base at IDR inflation, so the terminal rate only carries the years beyond the reserve life and is not a growth assumption for the mine.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 6.4% of revenue: the 9M2026 actual (S3), the last actual and therefore the calibration point under MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE. 9M2026 selling expenses of Rp262.7bn less the Rp228.5bn royalty inside them, plus administration of Rp134.1bn, plus the Rp29.6bn non-production site cost, over Rp3,107.4bn of sales = 6.4%. Royalty is modelled separately and D&A is a separate line, so both are stripped out to avoid double counting. The old 8.2% was the FY2025 ratio, when selling and non-production costs ran ahead of sales; holding it would have carried about Rp74bn a year of opex the last actual does not show.

challenges.challenge: FCFF is built as EBIT x (1 - a.tax_rate) with a.tax_rate = 12% (cov_engine explain --line fcff), but the EBIT being taxed is mining-only. The 12% is the consolidated effective rate precisely because the associate income sits below EBIT and is untaxed: 9M2026 tax Rp148.6bn on PBT Rp1,157.2bn less associate income Rp461.1bn gives 21.3% (S3 p.6), and the report itself states the mechanism in section 3 ('the associate income is taxed at the refinery, not at CITA'). On the mining effective rate, FY2026E FCFF falls from 609.9 to about 530 (-13%), the DCF EV from 7,017 to about 6,150 (-12%), worth roughly -200/share on the DCF and -120 on the 60/25/15 blend, i.e. a target near 3,010. The rating survives; the target and the DCF table do not.
challenges.answer: Mining effective rate 21.3% now applies to every forecast year and the long run: 9M2026 tax of Rp148.6bn on PBT of Rp1,157.2bn less the equity-accounted Rp461.1bn gives 21.35% [S3]. One engine rate taxes the whole pre-tax line, so the forecast profit line is conservative by the tax on the associate line; section 3 states the LK-basis profit and the payout is set on that basis.

challenges.challenge: The associate is 26.5% of the DCF equity value (3,642.1 of 13,750.1) and 46% of FY2026E net profit (620 of 1,341), but the DCF's FCFF excludes other_nonop entirely (formula: ebit*(1-tax)+da-capex-nwc), so the associate's earnings power has exactly zero effect on the DCF - a one-third change in the normalised contribution moves the DCF by Rp0. Section 4 claims 'if the normalised contribution is a third higher or lower, the value moves less than the ore price does, because the associate is carried at book in the bridge and only its flow through the profit line changes the DCF'; the flow changes the DCF by nothing. The report's own note that book 'understates the earnings power of a refinery that earns a high return on its asset base' contradicts keeping the same book mark inside the 60%-weight primary. The variant view - the associate is normalising, not dying - is therefore not in the valuation at all.
challenges.answer: The 30% WHW stake is now valued on earnings: normalised contribution of Rp650bn capitalised at the 12.52% cost of equity less 3.4% terminal growth (11.0x) = Rp7,127bn, less the Rp3,642bn carrying value already in the pack's investments line, so the bridge carries the Rp3,485bn uplift only [S2][S3]. Section 4 states the per-tenth arithmetic because the engine's sensitivity grid is fixed by the industry config and cannot vary the associate line.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 says 'the two Sandai licences produced only 227.9 Mt'. F37 stores 227.858 with unit Mt, but its own quote (S2 p.78) reads 'pencapaian pada IUP 26 dan IUP 29 tercatat sebesar 11,25% atau 227.858 WMT' - 227,858 WMT = 0.228 Mt. The rendered figure is 1,000x too large, is eight times Indonesia's entire 2026 domestic output of 25-30 Mt (S4, F35) and exceeds CITA's total production of 4,705 kt (F4). The cross-check in the same paragraph confirms the correct value: Air Upas 4.47 Mt (F36) plus Sandai 0.228 Mt = 4.70 Mt = F4.
challenges.answer: F37 corrected to 227.858 kt (0.228 Mt) with the unit fixed; the cross-check now closes: Air Upas 4.47 Mt (F36) plus Sandai 0.228 Mt equals total production 4.705 Mt (F4) [S2]. Every other kt/Mt fact was re-checked against its quote and scale.

challenges.challenge: Six placeholders apply |pctv (value already in percent) to fraction-valued keys: val.konglo.compress.{base,bear,bull} and deck.konglo.prob_{base,bear,bull}. The engine's values are 0.20, -0.25 and 0.60 (fund record valuation.konglo.compress) and 0.50/0.25/0.25 (konglo deck prob_base 0.5), so the report prints 'the base regime closes 0.2% of it, the bear regime -0.2% and the bull regime 0.6%' in section 4 and 'probabilities of 0.5%, 0.2% and 0.2%' in section 5 - a 100x understatement. As printed, a reader cannot see how 3,393 becomes 3,130; the correct reading is that the base regime closes 20% of the log gap and keeps 92.3% of the value.
challenges.answer: The three compress keys now use |pct and render 20%, -25% and 60%, and section 4 states in words that the base regime closes a fifth of the gap [S7]. The three deck.konglo.prob_* placeholders were removed rather than reformatted: the deck defaults (0.5/0.2/0.2) are not the lens weights and do not sum to one, so section 5 states the model's 0.5/0.25/0.25 in words.

challenges.challenge: The summary calls 4,043 'our fundamental twelve-month value' and section 4 says 'The fundamental value is Rp4,043 per share before the liquidity discount and Rp3,393 after it'. Neither is the model. 4,043 is the base-scenario v0 today, with no probability weighting and no roll-forward; the probability-weighted value today is 3,936 (0.5x4,043 + 0.25x3,052 + 0.25x4,608) and 3,149 after the 20% discount; 3,393 is the 12-month probability-weighted value after the discount (fund record v0 / tp_fundamental / konglo.v_fundamental). 4,043 x 0.8 = 3,234, not 3,393. The frontmatter says the discount is 'mid-teens' (correct: 2,850/3,393), while the summary implies 29% (2,850/4,043), and the '0.91 of value' is price/3,149, not price/3,393 (0.84).
challenges.answer: Section 4 now defines the bridge once: today's probability-weighted value after the 20% discount is 3,531; the twelve-month weighted value is 4,768 before and 3,814 after the discount; the lens gives 3,211. The base-scenario v0 (4,497) and tp_base (4,883) are labelled as base case only, and the summary uses the same definition [S2].

challenges.challenge: The 25%-weight EV/EBITDA cross-check uses a 14.219x peer median applied to FY2025A EBITDA: fund record valuation.methods.ev_ebitda.metric = 776.755, i.e. last-actual spot-year earnings at a current peer multiple, which the commodity card forbids ('Never value a cyclical on spot earnings or current-year multiples - procyclical error #1'). The peer set, the multiple's date and its EBITDA year are not stated in the report, and the visible METALS_OTHER trailing EV/EBITDA dispersion (ALKA 7.2x, TINS 13.0x, MDKA 47.7x, PACK 1,949x) makes 14.2x non-reproducible from the report. The method sits 29% above the DCF (4,489 vs 3,472) with a quarter of the weight and the divergence is not explained.
challenges.answer: The peer set (our METALS_OTHER coverage group), the October review date and the FY2025A earnings year are now stated, the 29% divergence is explained as a procyclical artefact, and the weight is cut from 25% to 10% [S2]. The engine fixes the metric to LTM EBITDA, so re-basing to FY2027E is not possible without an engine change; section 4 states what the same multiple would give on FY2027E EBITDA and why that is the cycle.

challenges.challenge: share_change is 0.000 in every year with the basis 'no issuance or buyback disclosed; the free-float remedy is a controller sell-down, not new shares' - no source, and it is an assumption about an event that has not happened. The float must rise 4.79pp to 12.5% by 31 Mar 2027 (konglo registry; S7 supports only the 15% stages and contains no 12.5% threshold). A 4.79% new-share placement, the cheaper route for a controller, dilutes EPS about 4.6%; the report itself lists this branch in section 5 as a view-changing risk but no scenario prices it.
challenges.answer: share_change now carries a 2.4% one-off in FY2026E (half of the 4.79pp free-float gap, the new-share branch) with the sell-down branch sourced to the registry and the OJK rule [S7]; section 5 quantifies the full 4.79% dilution branch and states that the engine's constant annual rate cannot carry a one-off inside a scenario.

challenges.challenge: The cash build is cash[-1] + np + da - capex - nwc - dividends (cov_engine explain --line cash), and np includes the Rp620-989bn of equity-accounted income, so the model treats 100% of associate profit as cash. Section 3 itself says 'the associate profit is equity-accounted and only becomes cash when a dividend is declared'. Forecast net cash of 1,231 in FY2026E and 22,204 by FY2047E is therefore overstated, and the dividend cover is not demonstrated: the parent dividend of 186/share (Rp738bn) against mining FCFF of 610 in FY2026E is covered only by income the model has capitalised into cash. If WHW's distribution falls with its profit, the payout is not funded.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now shows the cover on cash actually received: FY2025 associate distributions of Rp1,344bn (F42) against parent operating cash flow of Rp461bn (F41), and FY2026E/FY2027E FCFF against the payout [S2]. The engine's cash line does credit the full associate profit, which overstates the forecast cash balance; that line does not enter the target, because the DCF discounts mining FCFF and net debt comes from the last reported balance sheet, and the report says so. The bear case cuts the payout.

challenges.challenge: The declared FY2025 dividend is Rp351/share (F32), a 12.3% yield at 2,850, and the commodity card calls the dividend 'the market's anchor' and requires a dividend-capacity yield versus NAV statement. The report never states the yield and never discusses that the base case embeds a 47% cut (351 to 186.26, 55% of a lower EPS). It notes the dividend is funded by associate dividends received but not whether 186 or something nearer 351 is the likely FY2026 payment; on FY2025's associate receipts of Rp1,344bn the higher figure is affordable. This is the largest omission on the bull side.
challenges.answer: The summary and section 3 now state the FY2025 yield of 12.3% at the current price, the base-case dividend of 176.5 against the declared Rp351, the reason for the cut (a reported profit about half the prior year once the associate normalises) and the affordability test on Rp1,344bn of associate receipts [S2][S3]. The nearer-351 outcome is carried in the bull case's higher payout.

challenges.challenge: The thesis rests on 'the fall is the normalisation of an alumina price spike the company itself flags in its annual report [S2]'.
